blocks.x: This is an interview with Bill Russell at Seminar Room 2 in the Harvard Tilton Memorial Library at Tulane University. This is Rio 1, the date is September 4th, 1962.

We'd been talking about some of the, this is Bill Russell again, some of the musicians that I'd interviewed at various times preparing for the book Jazz Man, and other times after that, that we weren't able to talk to because most of them are dead now. We weren't able to interview them for our Jazz Archive directly here. One of them was George Bach K., whom I stopped to see in Philadelphia in 1940, fall of 1940. The actual date was December 15th, 1940, on the way when I was moving to Pittsburgh. And he was playing at a little restaurant, not a little one, quite a big one really, called Wilson's Cafe, about 51st and Walnut. And I noticed out in front of the place they had a sign with his name, George Bach K.'s orchestra, spelt B-A-K-A-Y. And he explained that nobody could pronounce the French or Creole spelling of it, so that he just wrote it out phonetically in English. Incidentally, Bung Johnson's widow claims to be a member of the Bach K. family, and she spells it quite different than that, too. Not on anything to do with English, but it's entirely different to French or Creole spelling, whatever it is. I won't go over these notes because they're rather sketchy, too. They're better than some of the notes I took. But they weren't taken right there. I wrote them probably when I got back on the train on the way to Pittsburgh. So I'll write those out a little bit more fully and send those in sometime. And Mrs. Rankin can remind me if I'm slow on it. But they won't be lost. I also have a couple of pages of information on George Bach K., which I obtained from John Reed about 1943. He had gotten all of this before 1941 when he lived in Philadelphia. He was connected with RCA Victor at that time. Incidentally, John Reed was a jelly fan, too, and obtained some of the unissued jelly masters from Victor files. It might be possible. Some of those were reissued, too. The bootleggers in New York, Sam Meltzer and Bolentino. I think one of the two issued some of those unissued masters that had never come out on Victor. I don't know if we can ever obtain those.
What label?
They were on some of the either Biltmore or British Rhythm Society. They used all sorts of phony names on those.
They were bootleggers?

Yeah. For some reason, they called them bootleggers. It means that they were pirated. One of the labels is called Jolly Roger. And incidentally, Victor would press those things for those guys. They'd steal the Victor rights, you might say. They didn't steal anything directly because it wasn't the actual property. But they'd take the records off, copy them, and issue them on another record. And Victor was pressing their own material for other people, which they always refused to do if they knew it. But they never even bothered to check on it. But some of those things. Anyway, I was going to say that John Reed and his wife, Mary, Mary Caroli had been her name, were very close friends of Sidney Bechet. And he had arranged Sidney Bechet's recording for Victor. He had been there. We always called him in New York as his unofficial manager. Anytime they'd get a vacation, they'd go wherever Sidney was playing. There was one camp they used to call Camp Unity, which in those days had the reputation of being sort of a communist camp up in New York State. And Sidney would go up there, not that he was a communist. He cared anything about politics, as far as I know. But it was a left-wing camp. So he'd go up there and play in the summertime, maybe for a month or so, these camps. And John Reed recorded some of those bands on the job that Sidney played. And there's one thing which I promised, I hope I find it before I go. If not, I may get equipment up in Missouri that I can copy from. I'll have to later anyway, get a new amplifier. And I'll copy that if I don't get it done before, which Mrs. Rankin has asked about, a George Bakke and a Sidney Bechet duet that John Reed had recorded. On two clarinets, I believe. He might have played the sax. The time I heard George Bakke, he was playing tenor sax most of the time. Just a small, I have it in the notes, maybe four or five piece band. Nothing exciting at all. So anyway, Sidney Bechet had given the reeds one of his old clarinets. Once when he had so much trouble with his teeth, he thought he'd never play clarinet again. But then later, his brother fixed up his teeth, Dr. Leonard, and he did play. But anyway, they had one of his clarinets. One of them, I notice, has been given to the Jazz Museum here. But he undoubtedly had several clarinets. So we'll go over that Bakke. He looked like a sort of retired, successful businessman, you know. He was quite light in color and, oh, very dignified. And looked like he was, his health was well kept, you know. I mean, later on, I saw him when Bunk went to Philadelphia when he was on the way out, you might say, he'd gotten very thin and had been sick. And he came back here and died. Nobody ever really got to talk to him. That was about 1949, I guess. He came back here and died here within a year or so. And even had a sister here, and we tried to check on her last year. Got all sorts of rumors that she had a restaurant. For a while, they had a saloon up on the Rambart Street, South Rambart. But we gave up, finally, trying to contact any of the Bakke relatives. I'm afraid they were all gone. There was one cousin, rather a distant cousin, I'm afraid, George Henderson's wife, who gave us a little dope on George Bakke, too. Ramsey also had a very good interview on Bakke, which I double-checked the material on it. Not that I was trying to, but I mean all of his information. Checked pretty well with the things that he told Ramsey. Ramsey's interview was published in Downbeat. Quite a big article in Downbeat in the early 40s. After Jazzmen came out, we hadn't contacted him, I don't believe, before. Jazzmen was published. We didn't even know for sure where he was, although we'd heard rumors he was in Philadelphia. He had left the Creole band before the others, before Kepard and Big Guy, for instance, had taken his place after he left. There were all sorts of rumors about him leaving, that they had a big, more or less, disagreement someplace, and some of them were left standing on a railroad station, and others just walked off. I don't know what the story was. The story about George Bakke that is usually told too often not to be true. Evidently, this show that they traveled with, I can't think what it was. Was it the passing show? Anyway, that's all been written up, the show that he was with, one of the stage shows, Trixie Freganza, Town Topics, maybe that was it, something of that kind. Evidently, he had been her boyfriend. She seemed to fall for him. Who is that? For Bakke, Trixie Freganza.
How do you spell Freganza?
F-R-I-G-A-N-Z-A. Thank you.
Ms. Rankin will appreciate you.

Somewhere in my notes, I have an article when she died about, maybe in the late 40s she might have died, and I clipped that in the paper. I'll come across that. I don't think I put that in Tulane here anyplace, but we can get the dope on her life a little bit too. But the story, which is probably pretty accurate, because they'd always say, oh, they'd see me taking notes like Gigi Williams. Oh, no, you can't print that. You thought I was writing it up for an article or something. Don't put this down. But she locked him in a room once when the band was ready to leave town. She didn't want to lose him. So she locked him in her hotel room or something, and he couldn't get away. So I think that's when they sent for Big Eye. It was considered some sort of a scandal amongst the musicians, at least, and some of them didn't want to talk about it, not that it was anything unusual, I suppose, either, but it was in a way. So incidentally, George Barquet's brother, Scheele, passed for white for years. As early as 1937, when I was in California, a friend of mine, Campbell Holmes, I just have to remember the name, so he used to write for a tempo magazine, which was later sold out to Downbeat. It was a West Coast magazine, a music magazine like Downbeat. And he had tried to interview Scheele Barquet, but when he found out he was trying to write up something about his life for publication, he refused to talk to him. And anybody else that would go through town, and if he found out they were interested in New Orleans music, well, he'd clam up entirely. He wouldn't talk at all. He was a member of the white local out there. He'd played with Jimmy Durante when he went to New York. That band recorded for Jeanette, even. I think...
They had a colored local, too?
Out there? Oh, yes, they did out there. They finally went together with the... After a lot of controversy, they finally went together. In the... Around 1945 or so, I think they finally got together.
Not long ago.
Well, maybe it wasn't that long ago. Might have been...
Not San Francisco, just recently.

Yeah. But they'd gone together... Anyway, say, 10 years or so ago, quite a while back. Anyway, George Barquet's brother, Sheil, who wasn't as well-known as George, down here at least, had passed for white for years. I know Mineta says he met him once on Canal Street after he started passing, and he said, well, I like it better. I forget. I have that in some of the Mineta interviews. Some of that stuff I'll copy, too, later on, which is on tape. He likes it better. Mineta sort of, you know, he wasn't mad at him or anything. Sometimes they are offended if they... Like Bunk would be. Bunk... There was one story there... Not a story. I mean, the fact that... When Bunk was in San Francisco... He was declaring that it's with Ellington for years. Barney Bigard. He wasn't trying to pass, but he just wanted to join the... He's light enough to pass, too. His brother is a little darker here, Alec Bigard. Barney wasn't trying to pass or give up the family or deny the family and all, like some people like Bill Johnson, we mentioned. But he did want to join the white local at that time, which was separate in Los Angeles, because they could get good movie jobs. And in fact, Barney did get some movie jobs there, even when he was a member of the colored local. But it would have been easier with the white local. And there was quite a big article in Downbeat once, in which Barney did actually come out that when he was trying to join the white local, said he wasn't a Negro, that he was really French, and went through that line. And he just played with Ellington because Ellington had hired him and all that for years, for 13 years. So he was going to come to town. In fact, he did come to town in San Francisco with the white band. He worked with white bands Freddie Slack for a while. And somebody else, I forget the other band. So he was to play with Bunk Johnson. I remember my friend Bill Colburn asked Bunk, short him the story in Downbeat, is this true that Alec Bigard isn't a Negro? And Bunk, he was so mad, he said, read the article, he said, no, he's not a Negro, he's a goddamn nigger. And Bunk was so proud of his color, he was very black. And we'd say, I'd rather be as black as that stove than as white as that sink. I mean, he really was. Not that he was trying to sour grapes or anything, he was proud of his colors. He couldn't understand anybody that wanted to pass. But Minetta did, of course, Minetta's quite light. He could pass almost too at any time. Probably, probably, well, I've seen him walk in white places with, even with me, that nobody would, even the Roosevelt Hotel, the jazz club must, nobody would know he was colored. So, he said, made some remark to Scheel Bakke, well, I see you're on the other side of the fence or something of that kind. And Scheel said, yes, I like it better, I like it better that way. Meaning you get better jobs and all that. So, he evidently didn't want to talk to anybody, the same as Bill Johnson refused to talk to any contacts that I tried to make with him those last three or four years. But I'll go over those Bakke notes. There's nothing especially to tell. Here's a note about Trixie Fragonza. A note in the San Francisco, St. Louis newspaper told the death of Trixie Fragonza at the age of 78 in 1949 in Pasadena. They called her an old vaudeville trooper.
November the 29th?
Yes.

1949. It says here she was approximately later, 11 years older than George Bakke. I figured that out. To get on to a few other people that I used to talk to, the next one on this list was Johnny Dodds, whose notes I'll have to send. They probably are in a box of Baby Dodds notes, I think. I was always going to try to rewrite them. When I first met Johnny Dodds about 1936, I went to Chicago and I inquired if he was playing anyplace or where he was. All I knew about him, he'd been on some of the jelly roll records and especially the Louis Hot Fives. Of course, his name is called off. You couldn't miss that on that Gut Bucket Blues when Louis introduces all the numbers. So everybody knew Johnny Dodds was on quite a few of those early records. So at that time, he was playing at a place called the One Cent Club. It was out at, I think, Roger Park Elevator Station, which I don't believe is running now, in the west part of Chicago, either north or south, I'm not sure. The what? Roger Park.
R-O-G-E-R?

Yes. Right at the end of the line. You go to the end of the line and this place, the One Cent Club, it means that you buy one drink at the regular price and you get a second drink for one cent. It was during the Depression, of course. They had on big blue silk blouses with big long full sleeves, you know, sort of like clowns wear. Not that they were trying to make clowns out of them, but I mean, it was a special uniform they wore. A drummer, I believe it must have been, I'm not sure, unless I, until I look up my notes, if I did write it down, even I doubt that I did. Probably Tubby Hall and the pianist was another Alexander. I can't think of his first name, but it wasn't Charlie Alexander who had played with him on some of the early records. But as soon as I told him I had his old records and I said, I'm going to play a piece, see if you know what it is. Of all things, it was high society, which anybody ought to know, although in those days it wasn't the, the nuisance it is. Now they play it almost like they do the Saints Go Marching In. Bunk always got so sick of it in New York where everybody would request it. Oh, two or three times a night. Oh, here's a thing I might mention, which I wanted to try to get Johnny Wiggs talking more about the different styles that they played pieces in and the dances, the way they did things. A year or two ago, he was trying to tell me a lot of stuff about New Orleans Band, some real good stuff. Don't remember now exactly what it was about, but he said he'd tell me later. I'd always say, don't tell me now, you'll forget it when you get on tape and think you've told. Anyway, he couldn't think what it was. But here's one little point that's quite characteristic of New Orleans music. In the old days, I understand, they played almost everything twice. It would hardly ever be that they'd play a thing. If the dancers clapped at all, I used to question Bunk about this. Even, say, 15 years ago when I'd go to any dance that Bunk played down here or around here, the George Lewis or any of those bands would play, if the people clapped at all, they'd play it over again, sometimes almost as long, maybe even longer, but usually a little bit shorter. If they played maybe 10 choruses the first time, they might play five or six the next time. And they still do that, even over at Preservation Hall, I noticed I'm surprised. a couple of times this summer they'd get into that and people clapped, which they did maybe more enthusiastically than usual. They'd play those over again. So in New York when they'd have a certain thing like the Saints, that's where the Saints started getting popular. Louis had made the Saints, not really popular, but he'd made this record in 1937 or 1938 and it caught on in a way. It was in the jukeboxes, but still the other small jazz band, and the other so-called Dixieland band leaders didn't pick it up. Nobody else played it much. But Bunk had recorded it and then he played it in New York maybe six or seven times a night and all the other bands saw how popular it was and so they all started recording it and playing it.
I heard that song as a white religious piece.

Really? A religious group. The oldest record I ever came across was an old Paramount which wasn't anything very jazzy, you might say. a quartet. You know, a sacred quartet. But anyway, to get back to Dodds, I was surprised then, of course, that to me he was somebody famous. Anybody on the Louis Hot Five would be a famous musician. And he even had a sign out in the front. I was surprised that that was in the first big popularity cycle of Benny Goodman had just made his big hit out in California at the Palladium or someplace and starting to make these Victor records and the swing was just coming on. It was just a big rage. And Benny Goodman even that summer had become known as the world's greatest clarinetist. So they probably got the idea from that. They had this sign out on the little painted, hand-painted sign out in front, Johnny Dodds, the world's greatest clarinetist. I was sort of surprised to see that. But inside, he was probably, it wasn't a union job, I'm sure. Because all the time I knew him in New York, he was playing non-union jobs. He might have been a member of the union even up until the last because he made some records in 1938. But these were little three-dollar-a-night jobs or so, anything he could get. Sometime they'd, I think baby, that'll be in some of the baby notes that I have, they'd play for, oh, anything they could get maybe the cafe owner or the saloon owner, if they had a restaurant, would give them a bag of food or something like that. They'd even play for things like that during the break. Things were really bad and that's about how bad it was there when Johnny Dodds was playing this little trio job. So he invited me to his home next day. At that time, I was one of these dyed-in-the-wool record collectors, you know, which was pretty, well, they were a pretty bad set, including me, you know. I mean, all the interest in the way was collecting records like stamps, although, of course, I did like the music. I'm not trying to say it was better than the other collectors, but a lot of the collectors, unfortunately, just collect them like stamps. But I went to his house, of course, armed with a whole big box of records I'd picked up. I remember I'd been in Buffalo a couple nights before and picked up some of the Oliver Columbia records, which we found now definitely have Jimmy Noon on. So I took all the Oliver records I had with me, including the Jeanettes and O.K.'s, and he'd say, oh yes, that's me identifying, told who else was in the band, which in general checked with other people. Some of those Oliver records have never been definitely established about the bass, whether it's Bill Johnson on the bass or whether there's a bass sax on there played by some Jackson or, because you couldn't hear the bass anyway, much below middle C didn't record very well anyway. Bill Johnson sometimes played banjo. But anyway, when we got to the Columbia records, those four sides on Columbia like Camp Meeting Blues and the New Arlene Stomp and another tune that Piku has his name on some of those too, P. Rohn. Dodds would say, it's not me, the clarinet. I'd say, have any ideas of Jimmy Noon? I don't know, it's not me. It seemed, not that he was just self-centered or anything, but if it wasn't Johnny, he wouldn't even venture a guess as to who it was. He'd say, it's not me. And he did at least identify the ones he was on, which we knew pretty well then anyway, but at least I did confirm some of those personnels, which at that time weren't really generally known. But that was one of my main interests, not only just to hear him, but to try to establish those personnels and it was a record collecting trip that I was on. I also got to meet, I'll write up those other notes a little bit fuller than I have even in my other notebook about Dodds. And I also went to see Jimmy Noon about that time and especially the next year or two, around 37 and 38 I remember. I remember one funny thing I always have to laugh at, he was always so heavy, he's really fat. At one time he hadn't been working for a long time, which is the truth, he was in a bad shape financially, but I remember him saying, I'm starving to death, I'm just starving to death. And yet he was, must have weighed 250 or more. He wasn't very tall, so he maybe didn't weigh so much. But he always had usually a group with just a piano, maybe three or four players, no really organized. One year I did hear him in a place called Platinum Club where he had about an eight or nine piece band, might have been ten piece. Played for floor shows and all.
What's it in there?

Chicago. Chicago. Then later he went to Los Angeles and died out there and made some records with Ori, or maybe not records, he made some radio appearances for Orson Welles, which he only really knew Arlene's band, type band he played with, say six or seven pieces for many years. He made them for this group with Mud Carey and Zutty Singleton as the drummer. So I'll hunt up some of those noon notes which are very sketchy too, very unfortunately. Very little is known about his life. I mentioned about Norwood Williams. You might look up some notes on him right now if I can find them. He had been the guitar player in the original trio band that had left here probably around 1914. According to some of the books, including Jazzmen, that band had left here in 1912. But a few of them had been out there including Dink Johnson and maybe Bill Johnson had a little trio at first as far as I can understand out in Los Angeles. But the whole band with Keppard and all those pictures that are taken probably weren't really taken maybe as early as 1912. It might have been as late as 1914. If we could get somebody in Los Angeles to go over those newspapers we could find out more about it because they played for some of the prize fights out there.
What year was that?
Around 1912 to 1914 all those dates had been given. That's the same band with George Barquet.
What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case because Papa Lane will say the same that they played all the same tunes Tiger Rag. Incidentally, speaking of the Shiel Baquet who played with Papa Lane they played down here. Papa Lane had two or three so-called colored musicians who were so white that you couldn't tell. Shiel Baquet started passing down here of course when he played with Papa Lane. And he also played with Happy Schilling, a trombone player who's still living. We had a very good interview with him. He was so sick I didn't want to bother him when our Tulane project started. But we have a copy of his interview here which was arranged by Johnny Wiggs. Anyway, Happy Schilling used to laugh about his black and white orchestra. I think he tells that on the interview. And he had also a Shiel Baquet with his group. And both, I don't want to quote either one of them but I know they both seem to imply that Shiel Baquet was a pretty good composer and he used to help arrange they even thought he might have written some of those tunes which he probably never even claimed. But that might have been their first experience even with Tiger Rag. Possibly they talked like and all the Shiel Baquet would arrange those numbers sort of for us and neither one of those bands in those days bothered with music. And Shiel Baquet no doubt could read music and the... But anyway, Papa Lane especially and Mama Lane we'll call her will laugh at the idea of Nick LaRocca writing any of those tunes of course because they'll say, oh we played those so long before that Nick, well like Papa Lane tells us, Nick would come along and rehearse with us and sometime we'd take him out on a job we'd pay him the same as the others and we'd pay him the same as the others. Like it was a joke that they paid him but anyway they needed extra musicians and they'd pay him even if he couldn't play is what he was trying to say. and not that they were trying to run him down although there was no love lost between them I don't think because Nick made so many claims and they'd see him on television claiming that he originated everything and they started to make Mrs. Lane would make her sort of sick she'd get a little riled up but Jack Lane popped up and it seemed to bother him he'd just laugh at him say well let him talk let him talk so anyway some of those other bands both white and colored must have been playing at least as jazzy as the original Dixieland band sometimes it looks like Nick LaRocca's only point was that they used the word jazz on the records in all first and before that they were ragtime bands and therefore he originated jazz but I doubt myself that we have no evidence on records or anything else that can actually prove it they did play all these ragtime sheet pieces and there were a few blues maybe published of course before the original Dixieland certainly Handy had published a few blues and they probably weren't the first blues either Handy probably if you want to use the word stole more blues and things than Nick LaRocca did other ragtime pieces you might say but somebody had got them published and copyrighted sooner or later they would have been lost so I mean there's nothing to worry about the fact that they cashed in on them because somebody else would have if they hadn't so I can't see that it made much difference if you cashed in on them but to get on with Norwood Williams who was in that first Creole group we'll see here if I can figure out what he said in 1939 I learned from Bud Scott that Gigi I don't know how you would ever spell that I just spelled like G-E-E would say G-I-G-I yeah or it might have been G-I-G I don't know where that came from but anyway he lived in Watts down south of Los Angeles the suburb where they evidently had been the big Negro colony a lot of them from New Orleans Zoo Robertson lived down that way Jelly when he went out there I mentioned before he'd worked there at Leakes Lake an amusement park and Jelly's godmother lived down there too she was still living I never got to find her she'd been this woman he talks about sort of a voodoo queen not necessarily a queen but at least mixed up in voodoo so I went down and talked to him he was running a filling station and I took my copy of Jazzmen along to try to identify pictures and all and it says here they also had a photograph of the original Creole band hanging in the back room and they got it for me to look at it was in better condition than the one we borrowed from Bill Johnson's and it also I made a note it had no date on it Bill Johnson had had printed on his in hand printing 1912 but I'm quite skeptical of that date that band was actually together in that exact personnel at that time they possibly had played together most of those fellows down here as early as 1912 but I think 1912 was about the date that Dink and Bill went out to California and had maybe a string trio for a while and they sent for Keppard and Barkay and all a and here it says Williams was enthusiastic about Buddy Bolden remembering the Take It Away I played him that Jelly's the general record of that Buddy Bolden's Blues as Jelly called it Bolden's He said he had played with Bolden's He said he had played with Bolden's He had been a member of Bolden's Troubadours which is a name we've never heard of much anyplace else as being called the Bolden Troubadours He implied the Bolden Troubadours had traveled as if it might have been part of a show which we've never come across any information to confirm that He said Bolden had started in 1890 ! 1890 and had played in Audubon Park along with Ori and Bud Scott and Mutt the group that were out there he confirmed the story that Bolden got his jazz from hearing spirituals at church He said it was a Baptist church where the shouts were performed The shouts of course were sort of sometimes called ring shouts where they would even dance around in the rings not necessarily in here even over in the Carolinas and Georgia and all that through the south but it was rather a lively type not the slow type of spiritual I understand as say Go Down Moses it was a jumping type that they call Mahalia calls gospel music today It says it was at the Baptist church where the shouts were performed so energetically the church became nicknamed The Gymnasium Incidentally it reminds me out there that when I was there in those years around 1940 there was one church they told about there in Los Angeles they used to dance so much they knocked it off of the foundation One of the musicians told me that and another friend confirmed that Adrian Tucker They didn't knock it knock it down they just shifted off of the say the rock or brick foundation probably they just knocked it over got shaken so anyway they called this church where Bolden went which we've never been able to identify or locate here the Gymnasium Williams mentioned the tune I'm going when Jesus calls me as one that inspired Bolden I'm going when Jesus calls me I don't remember ever hearing it and we've never checked up we slipped up on those things really we should have been asking people I should have gone over these notes several years ago Williams told me what a powerful and expressive coronet Bolden was it may not be good English but it's the way it's written and how jazzy he was compared to Louis who might be regarded as a great novelty player Bolden really played jazz a lot of the old timers think that Louis played a lot of fast runs and

You were talking about... Yeah, a lot of the Negroes down here, they're all crazy about him. They all try to imitate him. And yet occasionally you run across some of the old timers that'll say, well, he plays novelty music. It's not really good jazz. Of course, all the young record collectors, and especially, say the ones...

Yeah, we should have been using about one reel of the good tape to get the guy's voice preserved, provided it's worth preserving, and then after that put it on the other tape, because this other tape lasts pretty good when it's air conditioned, I think. It used to go to pieces. I've had tapes that I've recorded. It's actually gone to pieces in seven or eight years' time. The life was only good for five years. Even the factory, they wouldn't tell that, but they knew that. Do you think it's better now? It's better now. It's pretty tough. It'll probably last, oh, it could last almost indefinitely. John Steiner advised me.

We're going through the Jelly Roll Morton. I can't talk at all sometimes. The Jelly notes in my notebook. First of all, I have a lot of things copied, like that big letter he wrote, the downbeat, and also the Afro-American in Baltimore. When Handy wrote an article saying he had invented the blues, and Jelly told him he'd heard more blues back here on the old junk man's horn than Handy would ever know. Incidentally, Johnny Wiggs' interview, he raved about those junk men, which I guess we'll never get to know now. The great big long horn, like a New Year's horn, that they'd play the blues on. They must have been terrific, because Johnny's never forgotten. The only other person that ever rivaled them was Joe Oliver, according to Johnny, which is about as high praise as Johnny can make.
Do we have copies of this material here?
We must have, if Mrs. Rankin or somebody can check on, if we don't have this Jelly letter in the old downbeat, if it's republished in downbeat, we must have it.
We have it.
All right, don't waste any more time on that.
And Handy, yeah, sure. I don't know, I've been through those things.

Yeah, so many people talk to Jelly, and there's so much stuff written in that Lomax book, which has a lot of wonderful material in it, as well as all the Library of Congress, so I don't want to waste a lot of time going over this.
I'd like to know what your personal opinion of his personality was.

I'm like, I believe, with all the musicians, and most of the better ones, you'll hear some awful reports occasionally, some musicians will say, oh, he was terrible. For instance, when we went to try to get, when Bunk came here in 1942, we went down to see Fats Pichon, Walter Pichon, who's probably a very nice guy, and I was prejudiced against him because when Bunk went and asked him to record with him, he refused. I guess it was going to be a non-union date. The union, of course, meant nothing to Bunk and all. I guess Walter was in the union and didn't want to do it, but the Bunk union, nothing meant anything except music in the first place and then friendship. I mean, Bunk was a 100% man. You hear all these awful sloppy stuff all about Bunk. It's disgusting to me. It doesn't really make much difference because nobody knows who he is hardly anymore, but I mean, Bunk was a wonderful guy. Bunk, if he was a friend, he'd do anything for you. I mean, you didn't have to be in the union to record or anything else if he wanted to record with somebody. But I mean, he didn't care if he was put out of the union. If some of his friends was going to do something, that's it. So he couldn't understand why Walter would have turned him down. I remember Walter at that time was talking something about Jelly Roll and running him down pretty much, or Jelly was just sort of a gangster who had a gun. And he was the only one that, Walter was the only one that Jelly was afraid of. Jelly, I think he claimed he put Jelly in his place once. Anyway, as if he was a very undesirable character, you know. He probably knew Jelly under some bad circumstances in New York, you know, when they didn't get along. But I mean, otherwise, I can't think of anybody, really any musician that, who I would call a musician, that ever knocked Jelly. There probably are some, and maybe I've heard things like that before, that he was hard to get along with, and that he bragged too much and talked too much. Some of them will laugh about that he was such a big talker. But practically everybody, like Simeon and all, say, no, I didn't see anything hard to get along with. Baby does, no, he was very businesslike and knew what he wanted, and he maybe would make Johnny play in the low register. Maybe he made Baby play with brushes when Baby didn't want to, but they wouldn't talk back to him. They had all sorts of respect for him. Like, as I mentioned, Judy Singleton. He wouldn't, no, I wouldn't be later, not with Jelly.
He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to be on that date, too. They wanted to line it up, you know, just like all of us make a lot of dumb mistakes and pick bands that maybe, with musicians that aren't necessarily suitable to play together, and the other, although certainly Jelly would have enjoyed playing with Louis and Sidney Bechet, and had wanted to, and his heart was sort of broken, that he couldn't. But he wouldn't do it, though, unless he could have been the leader. He would have a young kid about half his age, like Louis wasn't half his age, but consider when Jelly was somebody, Louis was a little kid, you know, in the home, maybe. And the same way with Sidney, although Sidney amounted to more at that time than Louis did, say in that 1910 period or so, or 15 period. Yet Jelly wouldn't have played as a side man with them. He was proud. I mean, he was, and figured he should have been the leader. And at least should have gotten paid as much as the other guys, as Louis say. But naturally, Decca at that time, I think, had Louis under contract, exclusive contract, and he, Louis was the leader of his band, and that's all there was to it. I know Charles Smith said it's sort of pitiful that Jelly was in the next, when they were rehearsing, Jelly happened to be in another, probably the NOLA studio or someplace, in one room rehearsing, and I heard the other band was in the, the whole New Orleans band was in the next room rehearsing, and Jelly was hoping he could be with him, but he couldn't. So they wouldn't pay Jelly anymore. They told Jelly he'd pay him a scale, and he was a side man, and that was it. Take it or leave it. And Jelly, of course, didn't have to take that, he'd starve before he'd take that kind of talk, so he wasn't on the date. So he was very proud, and in some cases, maybe hard to get along with too, but none of the greatest musicians I ever talked to, let me say the Dodds or Simeon or any of those that worked with him, Mitchell, oh no, Jelly is fine. No, I didn't have any trouble. No, I never heard he was hard to get along with. Mitchell will say, no. He maybe rehearsed and made him play certain things the way Jelly wanted him, but that was all. But anyway, this, I'll mention, I'll read a little bit of this. It was about, the winter of, spring of 1938 was one time, and another time, the winter of probably 37, that I first went to Sime. One time, I remember, I was with this Red Gate Shadow Players, and we, this one, Roosevelt at least, well, he was in the White House so long it could be any time, before 1944. Jelly was dead before he went. But I know one time, I was late setting up the stage. They were mad because I was out looking for records or else went to see Jelly. I forget what it was at the White House. I was much more interested in Jelly, of course, than the White House. But it was easy enough to find as long as you had the address there on U Street. I have here a note, the room is rather large but narrow. And as Charles Smith had told me, it was too brightly lit for a nightclub, mostly just a lot of high ceiling lamps. And he had only a little new spinet, quite a small piano against one wall and a jukebox back towards the kitchen. I drew a plan of it here. It was about, seven or eight tables maybe in the place. And when I told him, as I say, that I had all those old records like the Pearls and Wolverine while he hurried into the kitchen.
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.
Yeah, 1211 U Street.
Yeah.

He said, here's a man who knows all my pieces and all. He was very pleased. So after talking a while, he said he'd made so many records he couldn't remember all of them. He mentioned, at that time, we didn't know all of his records either and we still probably don't. But he mentioned he'd made some under other names and all too. But that might have been something like those Vocalions. He didn't have his name on all of those. Anyway, when the subject of Simeon came up and also about Earl Hines, that Simeon was working with Hines, he was disgusted that Hines, I mean that Simeon had to work with somebody like Hines, which might have been a little bit of jealousy, but still at one time he was considered a lot higher than Hines, I guess, back in the early Chicago days. So he thought that was a shame that he had to work with a guy like Hines. And he mentioned that Simeon was his favorite clarinetist. And he mentioned he'd also recorded with the Bach K. At that time we didn't know, I don't believe that he'd ever recorded with Bach K. So he went over his jukebox and put a nickel in and played a record, one of the New Orleans Bump, I think. It has some funny flutter tonguing in there on clarinet, which they don't do anymore. Incidentally, even George Lewis used to do it in New York around 1942. Five and Six. You never hear George do anything like that here, but do that same rough growling and flutter tonguing, which is, hardly ever anybody does it here, but Bach K. was doing it on that record all the way through one chorus. We never could find out any records that Jellie had made with Jimmy Noon, although he said he had made them. When I asked him which ones, he said Grandpa Spells, I believe. But we never could find them. But I'll copy some of these notes sometime, which I remember when I asked Jellie to play, he started talking about his left hand and all. He said players today don't have a left hand, of course, which is true if you take some of the fellows that just play up in the treble, with somebody where they're heard more. They don't do it. He probably has a pretty good left hand at that. But I mean, some of them got a style just playing up high where they're heard more and they don't do anything with the bass. But he was very proud of his left hand and always made a point of that. So I mentioned...
I don't know any other pianists in the... Do you?

No. Of course, he explains even, I think, on the Library of Congress that the piano is sort of a substitute for orchestra to a whole band and he seemed to... That may not really be a characteristic piano style to try to imitate. I don't think he was necessarily trying to imitate a piano but at least he was filling in everything, playing all the different parts which the piano can do. He told a little bit about the records he made with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. I think that's been pretty well covered in different magazine articles.
I have a note here. He mentioned that there were

three great clarinetists in New Orleans. Piku, Lorenzo Tio, and George Bakke. He didn't think Big Eye Louie was really in the first class. Other people will tell you they think Big Eye was better than Piku and so on. So some of that could be a question of opinion. he thought Dodds wasn't really a first class clarinetist. He was all right. He was only on a couple of his records, maybe four sides or so. I don't know. I even asked him once, I said, is it true that Muggsy had recorded with him? And he said, yes. No, I don't know. As I say, I believe that 99% of the time Jelly told the truth. I mean, any of this spreading on about how good he was, I never thought he had to spread it on. You couldn't exaggerate it, but it's possible in certain little cases, certain things, he might have said yes, you know, just quiet me down, too. If I said his Muggsy on, he thought, because it's possible, it might have been that Natty Dominic thing, though, too, or something, he had a tone similar to muted style at times. So I don't know whether that's really true that all these people recorded with him or not, because he had no reason especially to brag that they did record with him. He talked, I asked him about the Oliver record, that autograph, and he seemed quite excited about Oliver, and about the solo, you might call it. He said, my God, what a memory that man had. He said, I would play a piano chorus or something like King Porter or Tom Cat just once, and Oliver would take it and remember every note that he played. He said, you can't find a man like that today. So he had a lot of respect for Oliver, but Kepford was his favorite trumpet player, and he seemed to think that Bolden was plenty good too, although he liked Kepford better. Had a more jazzy style evidently. But I'll go over these notes sometime and copy everything here that's fit to copy. Some funny little stories, little remarks about Sidney Bechet. He thought he was great too. He seemed to like George Mitchell. I always wondered why he used somebody who wasn't from New Orleans when he could have had a pick of people you think like Kepford or Louie or other people around Chicago when he made those records. But he talked quite a bit, thought he'd learn a lot from Kepford and Oliver. Actually, Mitchell did, in his interview that we have of his claims, he learned a lot from Oliver. He tried to play like Joe. He said, I never could make it though. Couldn't quite make it like those New Orleans fathers. I tried my best to play like Joe but I didn't really succeed. But the jelly said, Mitchell's a greater carnettist than Louis Armstrong. But of course he'd say that about a dozen other people. Evidently, he didn't like Louis too well. They wrote one tune together, the Wild Man Blues. I wish I'd questioned him about that to see what part they wrote, how they wrote it together and all. I didn't get so many things we could have asked him. And the last time I saw jelly was up after I'd been to California a year or so. He came back and a friend of mine took me up to jelly. He'd been seeing him every week about it, Herman Rosenberg, a fabulous guy around New York, which is a whole story anyway. He's been written up in the papers. He's dead now. We went up to see Sidney Bechet who'd just gotten back from Chicago. They'd had a session for Victor in memory of Johnny Dodds. He made this date, Blues for You, Johnny, which is really a pretty sick sounding tune, I thought. One of the very worst records ever made. They took some popular singer along and sang it all the way through. I know Sidney gave me the supposedly original manuscript. I don't know where that is. I'll have to find it someday and we'll copyright it. I doubt if it's in Sidney's handwriting, though. Somebody else must have written it out for him. But he also played some opera stuff like the aria from Pagliacci, you know, the one that Caruso and all of them sing where you start out laughing and practically cry and all that stuff. And Sidney was wonderful. I mean, he's a dramatic player. He could play all that opera stuff and really make it sound. Then we went down to the rhythm club. I guess that's what it was called, a big place where all the musicians would meet a big pool hall, mostly, and back. Jelly was back there playing pool and we waited outside there, not that we were, it was segregated or anything, but somehow we just waited outside. About five or ten minutes after he finished his game, he came out and began talking. I was so dumb, and I still am, but he invited me to come the next Monday to a rehearsal where they were rehearsing a new band and all. Henry Allen, I think Paul Barberin was in for a while, and he was always trying to get a new band together. Somehow I never got to that rehearsal and a month later, Jelly left town, and a month later I left town, never did see him again.
He was dead in that two summer.

Well, yeah, the next summer, that was the fall of 1940, and he died in June. But he was talking how at that time he was still going to sue either MCA or he was suing ASCAP. He was always suing somebody for a million dollars, not paying royalties on his tunes. I mean, he had big ideas like that, exaggerated some things of that kind of, he wouldn't have been due a million dollars royalty, but he figured a lot of people were cashing in on his work, which they did. They never got to be millionaires, of course, but still they did, he didn't get much royalty. I don't doubt for a minute that he didn't get his full royalties out of his publications, but he was all excited about that. I was trying to tell him a few of his old friends I'd seen in California, people he played with, Howard, not Darnell Howard, but the other sax player out there who had a band, I can't think of his name, and a few other people, he thought they were great, in fact, he always had words of praise for almost everybody. Howard, he thought was about the best sax player, I can't think, Dick Allen would know his name instantly, I can't think, he's made a couple of records out there, with, not extra good, but a medium sized band, not a really big band. And other people, speaking of California, when I was out there, I tried to collect some information on Jelly, because his general album, the beautiful one that came out on Commodore later, had just come out, and Charles Smith knew that that time that the average reviewer in any music magazine would pan the thing, although surprising, a downbeat that time did give one of his vocals on, I believe, Mamie's Blues, that was one of the two or three outstanding vocals of the year, in blues vocals, they did like that. So Charles had supervised and arranged the sessions, so he arranged with this tempo magazine that I review the album. But even then, I'm not trying to knock Dave Stewart, he's a wonderful guy and a good friend, I mentioned that Dave came down and recorded Bunk for the first time at all, but I took that album around, I didn't have a phonograph, I had to take it over to Dave's shop to play, and whenever customers would come in, Dave would say, you better not play that, you might drive some of the customers away. And a year later when Jelly came out there, Dave got so crazy about Jelly that he was the only one that went to Jelly's funeral, and he was writing a book, I was starting to take down in longhand a dictation that book for Jelly, only got a couple of pages before Jelly got sick. So he was certainly the number one Jelly fan, but the year before when I brought that general album out, he said, don't play it in the store, when people are here, they chase out the customers. So you can see why Charles did want me to review it because he knew I liked Jelly. But anyway, I ran all over the town trying to find people that knew Jelly and dug up a few pictures at the barber shop, I believe Sutherland or somebody had a trombone player who played in the black and tan. People out there, some of those musicians didn't like Jelly because he was better than they were. As Minette will tell too, when the Ori's band went out, they had a lot of trouble, they'd try to chase him out of town. They'd have prohibition agents to rate him and all too because the fellas out there couldn't play that New Orleans style same way Chicago. They were getting all the work and all the crowds going. But I know one fella said that Jelly didn't get all those diamonds all just for music. They implied he was either a procurer or a pimp, you know. And possibly he had been mixed up in all the district. He might have been mixed up in some of the prostitution racket out there too, which I don't know that there's any evidence to that. But I mean they said that's where he got all of his diamonds and his money and his Cadillacs and so on or whatever he had.
Well he said don't leave me here. He said he's always had six, seven, eight, or nine. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Maybe they just gave him some.

Here's the name right here. Paul Howard is the greatest tenor that ever lived. But he used to have trouble with him. At first he couldn't play and all of a sudden he picked up and learned enthusiastic about anybody that he liked. So as I said that's the last time I saw him was there outside the rhythm club where he was all enthusiastic about his new band. But he was already sick and on the way out then I guess.
Maybe that's the reason he was a good band leader though to some
extent.
He got enthusiastic about the people he
came with.
Yeah that
enthusiasm would carry through.
Some of those red hot pepper pieces are really wonderful.

But I'll go over all these jelly notes and I don't think there's anything much more here I wanted to mention about him. Oh there's a little dope here from Bill Colburn and a good friend who liked musicians. When Leadbelly would go out there he'd have him live in his home just to try to learn about the blues when Bunk went out there. He'd known Bunk down here but he invited Bunk to live at his home. Some of that will be in the letters we have written from Bill Colburn's home on Columbus Avenue. Jelly used to go down and see Bill Colburn used to go down to Los Angeles just to see Jelly when he moved to California. Incidentally that album I said wouldn't sell or I had the review because they were going to chase customers out. Bill Colburn had that album he'd go all over town in San Francisco where he lived and play it for everybody and that got to be one of the best sellers in San Francisco. Sherman Clay couldn't keep enough of them there because everybody he'd play it for and he'd talk him into buying it.
A general album?

Yeah. So Bill would go down to see Jelly when he moved out there. He was already sick and could hardly play. And Bill would start to get Jelly talking. He'd prod him with things like he'd say, well you're alright but you can't play the stuff like Teddy Wilson. Teddy Wilson, I know you're good for that old time stuff but you can't play that new stuff you can't get around on the piano. Or like Art Tatum and all that. So once it got Jelly so burned up that Jelly said I'll play something those guys can't play and even when he was sick he went over to the piano Dink had a piano in his house I guess at that time and played the Finger Buster which nobody knew he'd ever recorded. He'd made a record on the but he said he played all that Finger Buster stuff. Incidentally this somebody was asking me the other day what I thought of Willie the Lion Smith or something and I said I never paid any attention to him. Much around New York used to hear him with Bechet but he brought out a record as if he'd composed it even later than that on Commodore called Finger Buster which is a pretty bad record same tune and all that Jelly I don't know when Jelly went out there he was trying to get up a band with Mutt Carey and all and Mutt had a job in some little I think called Silver Dollar little place down on about 12th Street and Main Street or he was I can't get all this story quite straight but nobody ever heard of Jelly out there for many years he hadn't been there for maybe 30 years or so and the boss wanted him to hire Jelly and told Mutt he better to hire him and all of them so they asked Jelly just who he was they sort of insulted him he said oh you don't know who I am hell you don't read the papers you know poor Jelly's name hadn't been in the papers for years but they thought that he thought everybody should know him I mean he still had that good opinion of himself I were his solos either so anyway he got pretty sick I guess when he was out there soon and wasn't able to play for very long but he actually had hoped to play when he was out there I know Roy Carew told me that even when he was in New York for that last band the one I missed rehearsing that he could tell he was just so ! sick then he would be saving his strength hardly playing with the band at all Roy knew him quite well enough to know whether he was really saving himself or not so he could take a solo chorus at that time they were having solos all the time of course but he must have been quite sick and quite weak out there incidentally I have a copy of his will someplace I haven't seen that I had a photostat made from I probably have just a negative of that which we can copy I don't know where all that material is now it must be here in New Orleans in some box I haven't seen it for many years anybody can go through the probate court files I have a copy it lying on top of the pile I have at home so I'll go through all those material things like that and I can send that will so we can get it photostatted if I don't come across it when I pack and I that Tony Jackson was the greatest pianist and the greatest and all that he'd ever heard but Jelly also knew of course he was good and said but my left hand enabled me to beat Jelly he made that statement once
beat
Tony
excuse

me but my left hand Jelly said this but my left hand enabled me to beat Tony so he thought he knew he had a little something probably that Tony Jackson didn't have too as Al Rose was saying the last time I saw him Al spent a lot of money recording a whole album of Tony Jackson music having Naki Parker play it hoping that he could recapture some of the style not knowing how Tony played either nobody does hardly now but it looks like Tony most of those pieces were not so hot so maybe Tony wasn't quite as great as some people thought he had this one big hit might have been a one tune this pretty baby of course might have been a one tune composer almost maybe
he was a good piano player but he wasn't much of a composer

yeah that's so true he must have been a great pianist but at least Jelly seemed to think here that he was of course Bunk always said too that Tony was the greatest he ever heard he even played Jelly claimed that's
what Jelly said about Mamie she just had one piece

yeah well I know that Tony could play more than one piece but I mean as far as composing that one was the only one that was really a hit he run contests Roy Carew I think that's all been written up though they had maybe dance contests whatever if it were the Lindy Hop or whatever was in style Jelly tried everything he could to get some life in that thing there
he was sort of managing this place he was
managing it and was supposed to be the emcee when they have a contest and the pianist he was the waiter though he'd wait
on was this a colored place a white place all colored segregated

probably all colored more or less segregated a few people like Charles Smith would go there though of course yeah a few other he had a few other people of course Lomax's I guess too or anybody like that that was around let me ask you a question

about when you think the so-called Dixieland revival began I've seen the statement as in this article here it began with the resurrection of Bunk Johnson it began 1940 it began old broom it began with Pee Wee Hunt and
all that
sort of thing
everybody's got a different date or different idea wherever they happened to be or whatever happened there must have been
some particular period there was

the time even when Lou Waters Band began recording out there in California that's before Bunk made any records at all that's the reason I think I mentioned the last time when Dave Stewart was going to record Bunk and Gene Williams rushed down there even if he were sick to talk over who should record Bunk because Dave had sold so many all the pressings he could make 10,000 he got and sold them all within a few weeks the jukeboxes even of Lou Waters out there and Lou had been playing that stuff for a couple years before that ever since 1937 or 8 when I first went out there he was maybe playing in a bigger band but he was trying to get small bands together making those arrangements and some of those fellas were actually record collectors too that's all I thought they were when I used to write to them I went out and found out they were musicians in Lou's band like Gerstbeck and the bass player and Ellis horn clarinetus all those fellas were
Turk Murphy there then oh yeah
Turk was there sure I heard
him play

they might not have all been working with Lou at that particular early period 1938 but Lou was getting little bands together so they were having Dixieland their so-called whatever you'd say out there I don't know I never did see it really die out like in Chicago Johnny Dodds and Baby Dodds all those fellas were working all the time and they made all those records like for Decca that session Louis Armstrong in a way had a sort of usually a big band but I mean he was playing some New Orleans music all the time and of course the little bands there nix all through the depression I remember Sharky going to New York in 1936 1936 and 37 when I first heard Brunus in 1936 I believe he was playing with Sharky yeah they were having little Dixieland bands I don't know
yeah

that's right he went up there I don't know that you could always hear music someplace like that maybe I don't know much of it before 1936 that I can remember around New York when they started a hot jazz club or something in New York there was more interest came up there in the 30s I would say

segments.title: Opening announcement, Tulane Jazz Archive, September 1962
segments.summary: Announcement of the interview with Bill Russell at Tulane, 4 September 1962.

segments.title: George Baquet in Philadelphia, 1940, and John Reed's bootleg labels
segments.summary: Russell recalls seeing George Baquet at Wilson's Cafe in December 1940 and the spelling of his name, then John Reed and the pirated Jelly Roll Morton masters.

segments.title: Baquet, Sidney Bechet, John Reed and the Trixie Friganza story
segments.summary: Russell describes Reed's ties to Bechet, Baquet's appearance and last years, his romance with Trixie Friganza, and brother Achille passing for white.

segments.title: Achille Baquet, Barney Bigard and passing for white
segments.summary: On passing in the white union local: Achille Baquet, Barney Bigard's attempt, Bunk Johnson's reaction, and Friganza's 1949 obituary.

segments.title: Meeting Johnny Dodds at the One Cent Club, Chicago
segments.summary: Russell visits Johnny Dodds in 1936 at a Depression-era club, with a digression on New Orleans bands replaying numbers and the Saints.

segments.title: Dodds identifies Oliver records; Jimmie Noone in Chicago and Los Angeles
segments.summary: Dodds's poverty and his identifications of personnel on Oliver records; then Jimmie Noone's later career and death.

segments.title: Dating the Creole band; Papa Laine, LaRocca; Norwood Williams on Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: Dates of the California Creole band, the Laine and Baquet bands against the Original Dixieland band, and Norwood Williams's 1939 account of Bolden.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong as novelty player
segments.summary: Fragment on how New Orleans musicians view Louis Armstrong, the old-timers calling him a novelty player.

segments.title: Tape quality and preserving interviews
segments.summary: Discussion of tape life and recording on good tape first.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton notes, Handy and the junk men's horns
segments.summary: Russell starts through his Morton notes: the Handy dispute and junk men's horns; what is already at Tulane.

segments.title: Morton's personality and what other musicians said of him
segments.summary: Fats Pichon's hostile view versus Bunk Johnson, Simeon and Baby Dodds's respect for Morton.

segments.title: Morton's pride, the Decca date and the visit to his Washington club
segments.summary: Morton refused a sideman role on Louis Armstrong's Decca date; Russell describes the room on U Street.

segments.title: Talking with Morton: his records, Simeon and his left hand
segments.summary: Morton's remembered records under other names, Simeon, flutter tonguing, and his piano style as orchestra.

segments.title: Morton on clarinetists, Oliver and Keppard; last meeting
segments.summary: Morton's opinions of clarinetists and trumpeters, Bechet, Mitchell and Oliver's memory; Russell's last sight of him outside the rhythm club.

segments.title: Morton's royalties and Russell's Morton album in California
segments.summary: Morton's lawsuits over royalties, Russell reviewing the Morton album, Dave Stewart, and rumours about Morton in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Morton's enthusiasm as bandleader
segments.summary: Paul Howard and Morton's enthusiasm for new bands, with agreeing remarks from the interviewer.

segments.title: Bill Colburn, Morton in California and Finger Buster
segments.summary: Colburn's friendship with Morton, his sales of the album, the Finger Buster story, Morton's illness and will.

segments.title: Tony Jackson and Morton's left hand
segments.summary: Tony Jackson as pianist and composer, Al Rose's album, and Jackson's job at a segregated club.

segments.title: When the Dixieland revival began
segments.summary: Russell on the revival's start: Lu Watters's band, Bunk Johnson, Chicago, New York in 1936.
